pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Holy Pascha: Midnight Procession around the Temple as a scored Sticheron (Tone 6). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: Byzantine-Slavic Hagiopolite & Stoudite Hymnographic Synthesis. Theological & Musical Significance: The monumental opening liturgical chant of the Paschal night, chanted repeatedly as the procession moves into the dark night.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L978–L981): ### Procession with the Holy Mysteries Around the Church After the taking of the Plashchanytsia from the Tomb and carrying it into the Sanctuary, the sacred ministers, having vested in all the brightest sacred vestments of their Order, go out before the steps of the Altar, and having all bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries, bend their knees, and take lighted candles; likewise also the Brotherhood in the church. The Deacon on the right (or the Priest himself, if there be no Deacons), having approached the middle of the Holy Table and bowed deeply, sets aside the Gospel on the right side thereof, and having taken the Holy Mysteries from the top of the Tabernacle (*Skynia*), and having placed them upon the Iliton, steps back a little to the side; and the Hierarch (or presiding Priest), having censed the Holy Mysteries thrice according to custom, and put on the Omophorion, standing up and ascending the steps, and having bowed down, receives the Holy Mysteries from the hands of the Deacon, turns toward the people, and when he begins to sing the Sticheron **"Jesus is risen from the tomb"** (*Воскре́съ І҆исꙋ́съ ѿ гро́ба*), while all the bells chime joyfully, the Procession around the church takes place, in all respects as was depicted on Great Friday at Vespers, here on page 445, except for the Plashchanytsia, which here, by order of Cardinal Sembratovych of blessed memory, is not to be carried, because it does not agree with the joy of the Resurrection; rather, it is fitting to carry the Icon of the Resurrection, as the Triodion has it at the beginning of Paschal Matins during the Procession to the church doors. And when the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Jesus is risen from the tomb"**, the Choirs and the people follow in singing the same, and they sing it, repeating it until the Procession is completed, that is, a threefold, or at least a single circuit around the church, which when it is completed, all enter into the church, while the banner-bearers and icon-bearers remain before the church doors to avoid commotion during the second Procession; while in the church the cross-bearer with two candle-bearers, the Brotherhood, the Choirs, and the Clergy arrange themselves for the Procession; and when the sacred ministers have entered into the Sanctuary, the Superior ascends the Altar, and having turned toward the people, blesses them with the Holy Mysteries, saying in a gentle voice: **"Save, O God, Thy people, and bless Thine inheritance"** (*Спасѝ, Бо́же, лю́ди Твоя̀, и҆ благословѝ достоя́нїе Твоѐ*); and having set down the Holy Mysteries upon the Altar, he descends before the steps, bends his knees, and having laid aside the Omophorion, censes the Holy Mysteries thrice according to custom; and the Deacon, having approached the Holy Mysteries and bowed deeply, removes them with the lunette from the Monstrance (*Darookazalnytsia*), and places them into the Tabernacle (*Kivot*), and the Tabernacle (*Kivot*) into the Ark (*Skynia*), and having bowed down, closes it. And where there is no Monstrance (*Darookazalnytsia*), the Holy Mysteries are exposed with the Tabernacle (*Kivot*), and with it are closed in the Ark (*Skynia*). *Note.* This Procession with the Holy Mysteries before Paschal Matins is a later adornment of our Churches, borrowed neither from the Greeks nor from the Romans, but from the Latin Churches of these regions, and an added magnificence to our Paschal Matins; nor is it set down in our Typika.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L978–L981): ### Procession with the Holy Mysteries Around the Church After the taking of the Plashchanytsia from the Tomb and carrying it into the Sanctuary, the sacred ministers, having vested in all the brightest sacred vestments of their Order, go out before the steps of the Altar, and having all bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries, bend their knees, and take lighted candles; likewise also the Brotherhood in the church. The Deacon on the right (or the Priest himself, if there be no Deacons), having approached the middle of the Holy Table and bowed deeply, sets aside the Gospel on the right side thereof, and having taken the Holy Mysteries from the top of the Tabernacle (*Skynia*), and having placed them upon the Iliton, steps back a little to the side; and the Hierarch (or presiding Priest), having censed the Holy Mysteries thrice according to custom, and put on the Omophorion, standing up and ascending the steps, and having bowed down, receives the Holy Mysteries from the hands of the Deacon, turns toward the people, and when he begins to sing the Sticheron **"Jesus is risen from the tomb"** (*Воскре́съ І҆исꙋ́съ ѿ гро́ба*), while all the bells chime joyfully, the Procession around the church takes place, in all respects as was depicted on Great Friday at Vespers, here on page 445, except for the Plashchanytsia, which here, by order of Cardinal Sembratovych of blessed memory, is not to be carried, because it does not agree with the joy of the Resurrection; rather, it is fitting to carry the Icon of the Resurrection, as the Triodion has it at the beginning of Paschal Matins during the Procession to the church doors. And when the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Jesus is risen from the tomb"**, the Choirs and the people follow in singing the same, and they sing it, repeating it until the Procession is completed, that is, a threefold, or at least a single circuit around the church, which when it is completed, all enter into the church, while the banner-bearers and icon-bearers remain before the church doors to avoid commotion during the second Procession; while in the church the cross-bearer with two candle-bearers, the Brotherhood, the Choirs, and the Clergy arrange themselves for the Procession; and when the sacred ministers have entered into the Sanctuary, the Superior ascends the Altar, and having turned toward the people, blesses them with the Holy Mysteries, saying in a gentle voice: **"Save, O God, Thy people, and bless Thine inheritance"** (*Спасѝ, Бо́же, лю́ди Твоя̀, и҆ благословѝ достоя́нїе Твоѐ*); and having set down the Holy Mysteries upon the Altar, he descends before the steps, bends his knees, and having laid aside the Omophorion, censes the Holy Mysteries thrice according to custom; and the Deacon, having approached the Holy Mysteries and bowed deeply, removes them with the lunette from the Monstrance (*Darookazalnytsia*), and places them into the Tabernacle (*Kivot*), and the Tabernacle (*Kivot*) into the Ark (*Skynia*), and having bowed down, closes it. And where there is no Monstrance (*Darookazalnytsia*), the Holy Mysteries are exposed with the Tabernacle (*Kivot*), and with it are closed in the Ark (*Skynia*). *Note.* This Procession with the Holy Mysteries before Paschal Matins is a later adornment of our Churches, borrowed neither from the Greeks nor from the Romans, but from the Latin Churches of these regions, and an added magnificence to our Paschal Matins; nor is it set down in our Typika.

And when the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Jesus is risen from the tomb"**, the Choirs and the people follow in singing the same, and they sing it, repeating it until the Procession is completed, that is, a threefold, or at least a single circuit around the church, which when it is completed, all enter into the church, while the banner-bearers and icon-bearers remain before the church doors to avoid commotion during the second Procession; while in the church the cross-bearer with two candle-bearers, the Brotherhood, the Choirs, and the Clergy arrange themselves for the Procession; and when the sacred ministers have entered into the Sanctuary, the Superior ascends the Altar, and having turned toward the people, blesses them with the Holy Mysteries, saying in a gentle voice: **"Save, O God, Thy people, and bless Thine inheritance"** (*Спасѝ, Бо́же, лю́ди Твоя̀, и҆ благословѝ достоя́нїе Твоѐ*); and having set down the Holy Mysteries upon the Altar, he descends before the steps, bends his knees, and having laid aside the Omophorion, censes the Holy Mysteries thrice according to custom; and the Deacon, having approached the Holy Mysteries and bowed deeply, removes them with the lunette from the Monstrance (*Darookazalnytsia*), and places them into the Tabernacle (*Kivot*), and the Tabernacle (*Kivot*) into the Ark (*Skynia*), and having bowed down, closes it. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Byzantine Hymnography and Church Monody in the Ukrainian Reception of the Early Modern Period
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The work offered to the reader is the first attempt in Ukrainian historiography to trace the formation of scholarly conceptions of Byzantine hymnography and church monody. New views on the Slavonic translations are critically examined; the repertoire of the oldest Slavo-Rus liturgical books, particularly the notated ones, is delineated.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Holy Pascha: Festal Matins (following Ode 3) & Midnight Office as a scored Hypakoe (Tone 4). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: Byzantine-Slavic Hagiopolite & Stoudite Hymnographic Synthesis. Theological & Musical Significance: The venerable proper response detailing the arrival of the Myrrhbearing Women at the tomb before dawn.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

pillar_1_significance.why_featured_assessment: Restores the second structural unit of Romanos's poem describing the Sun before the Sun seeking dawn in the grave.
pillar_1_significance.liturgical_role_and_context: Assigned to Holy Pascha: Festal Matins (following Kontakion) as a scored Ikos (Tone 8). Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: St. Romanos the Melodist (6th-c. Constantinopolitan Kontakion tradition). Theological & Musical Significance: Restores the second structural unit of Romanos's poem describing the Sun before the Sun seeking dawn in the grave.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Computer Database of the East Slavic Heirmologion (Irmos)
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

Hymnographic Attribution & Lineage: Byzantine-Slavic Hagiopolite & Stoudite Hymnographic Synthesis. Theological & Musical Significance: The supreme luminous automelon of Pascha, sung thrice by the clergy in the center of the illuminated temple.
pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. pillar_1_significance.typikon_rubrics: Isidore Dolnytsky, *Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои* (Lviv, 1899), `1899_dolnytsky_part4_triodion.md` (L983–L987): ## Paschal Matins 1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620] 2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Paschal Matins

1. **Procession Before the Church Doors.** As all the people go out from the church, the sacred ministers likewise go out after them, and the Procession takes place thus: when the sacred ministers have taken their stand, in all their bright sacred vestments, before the steps of the Holy Table, the Superior takes the Cross, and the Deacon the Censer; and when all have bowed equally and deeply toward the Holy Mysteries and turned toward the west, the Superior begins to sing the Sticheron **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ Savior"** (*Воскресе́нїе Твоѐ, Христѐ Спа́се*); and while all follow in singing the same, they go out from the Sanctuary, the Priests indeed through the Royal Doors, and the other sacred ministers through the Deacon's Doors into the church, and while all the bells are ringing, they go even unto the great Church Doors; and having gone outside the church, they stand orderly, facing the church doors, which are immediately closed.[^619] And inside the church there are placed upon the Holy Table, first of all the Icon of the Resurrection of Christ, usually upon the Artos, and other venerable Icons, and Reliquaries, and the most precious Gospels, or whatever else of sacred things, all these according to the number of Priests who intend to give them to the people to kiss at the end of Matins; while outside before the church doors the beginning of Matins takes place thus.[^620]

2. **Beginning of Matins.** Immediately upon the closing of the church doors, the presiding Priest, holding in his left hand the Cross, and in his right the Censer, and censing the church doors,[^621] proclaims with a loud voice: **"Glory to the holy..."** (*Сла́ва ст҃ѣ́й*), and the rest.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Matins Chants in Ukrainian Irmologia of the 17th–18th Centuries
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: It is important to note that the special significance of monophonic liturgical singing lies in its inseparability from the liturgical texts, the symbolic content of which embodied the most important dogmas of Christian doctrine. In this context, an important role was assigned to the Matins service, which symbolized the light of Christ’s Resurrection and thus confirmed the fundamental postulate of Christianity – the immortality of the human soul. Therefore, the study of the repertory of Matins chants from the standpoint of their liturgical fullness is particularly relevant, as in this way we obtain testimony not only of their theological but also their artistic value. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Kyivan Square Notation System and Stylistic Layers of Ukrainian Monody
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The core theoretical thesis of our research is that **Kyivan notation in its early operational stage functioned as an autonomous relative pitch system**. It recorded not absolute pitch frequencies (which characterize post-Renaissance mensural and modern metered notation), but rather the modal, intervallic, and melodic-contour relationships between scale degrees within a mobile solmization grid.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Incipitary of the 1709 Lviv Stauropigian Printed Irmologion
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: May 15, 2009, marks 300 years since the publication of the second edition of the staff-notated *Irmologion*, prepared at the press of the Lviv Dormition Brotherhood by the printer Vasyl Stavnytskyi. In content, artistic decoration, and general elegance, this edition significantly surpassed the *Irmologion of 1700*, which came from the press of the St. George Monastery[^1].

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. This Feast does not have an All-Night Vigil, nor a Polyeleos at Matins, but only the Great Doxology; while at Vespers there are both Entrance and Readings. *Note.* This Feast is a Feast of the Lord, eight-day [an Octave], beginning with the Wednesday of the Paralytic, and ending with the Wednesday of the Samaritan Woman, on which it also has its Apodosis. On the Feast itself, and at the Apodosis, the Service of the Feast alone is sung, while the Service of the Saint of the day from the Menaion is sung at Compline; but on the other days it is combined with the Menaion, except on the Sunday of the Samaritan Woman, for then it is combined with the Service of the Sunday. This Feast does not have an All-Night Vigil, nor a Polyeleos at Matins, but only the Great Doxology; while at Vespers there are both Entrance and Readings. We begin its Service from Tuesday evening, for the Church day begins from the evening of the preceding day.

#### Order of the Feast

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

### The Ascension of the Lord

This Feast extends over 9 days; for it reaches even unto Friday after the Sunday of the Holy Fathers, on which it also has its Apodosis.

The Feast, the Afterfeast, and the Apodosis of the Feast we celebrate according to the General Rule of a Feast of the Lord; only at the Liturgy our Sluzhebnyks, in place of **"We have seen"** (*Ви́дѣхомъ*), and in place of **"Let our mouths be filled"** (*Да и҆спо́лнятся*), appoint the Verse: **"Be Thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and Thy glory over all the earth"** (*Вознеси́ся на небеса̀, Бо́же, и҆ по все́й землѝ сла́ва Твоя̀*), which we say even unto the Apodosis; and on the following Sunday of the Holy Fathers, the Service of the Ascension has a proper Typikon, for it is combined both with the Resurrectional Service and with that of the Holy Fathers, as follows.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: The Liturgical and Musical Dimension of Great Vespers in Ukrainian Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Relevance of the Topic. Ukrainian sacred art has long occupied a prominent place in national culture. The Church and its creative inspirations, especially in the early modern era, were an important factor in the formation and development of artistic progress, and in this a great role belongs to the sphere of liturgical chant. The core of the Ukrainian church chant tradition is monophony, or the ancient medieval monodic practice, whose roots reach back to Byzantine liturgical rite. Thus, sacred monody is evidence of continuity and, at the same time, a solid foundation for the development of the national spiritual art. With the introduction of polyphony into liturgical practice, monody did not lose its significance and remained the basis of the divine services of the daily cycle, which begins with Vespers. Therefore, the study of the chant repertoire of Vespers is relevant first of all from the standpoint of the historical reconstruction of the foundations of Ukrainian liturgical rite. As a result of the reform of notation—the introduction of the five-line form of notation—innovative staff-notated liturgical collections emerged in early modern Ukraine, namely the irmologia, which also included the repertoire of Vespers. A precise reading of these chants makes it possible to obtain an authentic record of the chant palette of the sacred rite. All this allows us to reconstruct a real picture of the Vespers service of the Baroque era in the context of the artistic significance of church life, the study of which is relevant for various reasons. On the one hand, Baroque art is evidence of the adaptation of the Byzantine liturgical repertoire and the reinterpretation of its chant forms, and on the other hand, a contemporary vision of the spiritual development of Ukrainian culture is impossible without taking into account the monodic sacred stratum. typikon_provenance.authority: Isidore Dolnytsky (1899 Типикъ Церкве Руско-Католическои, Lviv)
typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
### The Ascension of the Lord

This Feast extends over 9 days; for it reaches even unto Friday after the Sunday of the Holy Fathers, on which it also has its Apodosis.

The Feast, the Afterfeast, and the Apodosis of the Feast we celebrate according to the General Rule of a Feast of the Lord; only at the Liturgy our Sluzhebnyks, in place of **"We have seen"** (*Ви́дѣхомъ*), and in place of **"Let our mouths be filled"** (*Да и҆спо́лнятся*), appoint the Verse: **"Be Thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and Thy glory over all the earth"** (*Вознеси́ся на небеса̀, Бо́же, и҆ по все́й землѝ сла́ва Твоя̀*), which we say even unto the Apodosis; and on the following Sunday of the Holy Fathers, the Service of the Ascension has a proper Typikon, for it is combined both with the Resurrectional Service and with that of the Holy Fathers, as follows.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

### The Ascension of the Lord

scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: Ukrainian, as well as Belarusian, sacred monody is one of the brightest links of the Byzantine cultural space of the early modern era, which for the first time paved the way for rapprochement with New European culture. Already at the end of the sixteenth century, it was precisely in Ukraine and Belarus that, for the first time in the liturgical chant of the Byzantine rite, they fully transitioned to European five-line staff notation for recording musical texts, adapting it to their own practice. The new method of notation not only testified to the significant stylistic evolution of Ukrainian-Belarusian church chant, but also stimulated this process even further. At the same time, the entire repertoire, whose roots went back not only to Kyivan Rus', but also to the Balkan Slavs and, naturally, Byzantium, was transferred to the new system of recording musical text.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Kyivan Chant in the Context of 17th–18th Century Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The main branch of Ukrainian church monody - Kyiv chant - has more than a thousand years of history of existence. Its origins date back to the period of the official acceptance of Christianity by Kievan Rus' at the end of the 10th century, and possibly even to the 9th century when the first Christian churches appeared in Kyiv. In the middle of the 11th century, with the division of the Universal Church into Eastern and Western, Kyiv chant (of course, it did not have this name then) was definitively established as a branch of Slavic vocal art in the Orthodox Greek-Byzantine area. From its inception, the tradition has been continuous: strengthening or weakening, it constantly revived and acquired new qualities in different epochs.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Cherubic Hymns of the Suprasl Chant in Staff-Notated Irmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Cherubic Hymn *Izhe kheruvimy* is one of the most important and oldest chants of the Byzantine Church, which from a musical perspective has undergone numerous changes and re-interpretations over a long period. The hymn is sung during the Divine Liturgy, that is, the Liturgy of John Chrysostom, which is the logical conclusion and culmination of the complete daily cycle of liturgical services. Therefore, this hymn is performed practically daily throughout the entire church year, with the exception of certain days of Great Lent. This explains, in particular, the extraordinary popularity of the Cherubic Hymn in composition, from the Baroque era to the present day.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Modern Chant Preservation and the Galician Oral Samohlasen Tradition
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: In reality, an immense role in this process belongs to the parish cantor (*diak*) and cantor-teacher (*diako-uchytel*)—a role that is all too infrequently emphasized in our contemporary era. The responsibility of the church singer is profound in preserving tradition: not only in terms of whom he trains to sing, but fundamentally *what* he teaches, what musical foundation he selects, and what he passes down to succeeding generations.

typikon_provenance.verbatim_source:
## Sunday of Pentecost

1. The Service of this Feast is celebrated over seven days, for it has its Apodosis on the coming Saturday. It has this proper feature, that on Sunday evening at Vespers toward Monday the Kneeling Prayers are read; and on the morrow, that is, on Monday, the entire Service of the Feast is sung without the Menaion, and at the Liturgy also the Service of the Holy Trinity, if desired,[^658] as we indicate immediately.

All the rest, from the Feast even unto its Apodosis, is performed according to the General Rule of a Feast and Inside a Feast of the Lord. At the Liturgy, **"As many of you as have been baptized into Christ"** (*Є҆ли́цы*), only on the Feast.

scholarly_summaries.study_title: Festal Stikhira Repertoire in Early Modern Ukrainian Heirmologia
scholarly_summaries.translated_summary: The Ukrainian type of Heirmologion as a unified notated liturgical book emerged approximately in the second half of the sixteenth century. Its universality ensured for this type of collection a flexible adaptability to liturgical practice. The Heirmologion also became a unique example of a large-scale all-Ukrainian reform, when, within a short period and literally across all the lands of the Ukrainian ethnos, not only was the optimal chant material selected, but it was also transferred from the ancient znamenny notation to the new five-line staff notation.
